title: Slack keeps breaking my focus: how to stop interruptions on Mac for product managers
metaTitle: Slack keeps breaking my focus? Fixes for product managers on Mac
description: Slack keeps breaking your focus? Set Focus and Slack working hours on your Mac, batch checks, and cut the pings you do not need this week.
intro: Slack keeps breaking your focus because it alerts you the moment a message lands, and your Mac adds its own pings on top. You can cut most of it with three built-in settings: a Focus schedule on your Mac, Slack working hours, and timed pauses with /dnd.
tldr: Set a Focus schedule in System Settings > Focus so Mac alerts stop during deep work blocks.
Set Slack working hours in Preferences > Working hours so messages wait for your time.
Use /dnd for a one-off pause, such as /dnd for 15 mins before a design review.
Batch Slack checks at set times, then judge the change by your own focus ratings for a week.

blocks.text: Why Slack keeps breaking your focus

Slack does its job well. It delivers a message the moment someone sends it. For a product manager, that means a question that could wait an hour arrives during the one hour you set aside to write a spec. Your Mac adds its own alerts on top, so your attention gets cut into small pieces all day.

Microsoft's 2025 Work Trend Index puts rough numbers on this. Its survey data says the average knowledge worker gets 153 Teams messages per weekday. Microsoft also says Microsoft 365 users are interrupted about every two minutes by a meeting, email or notification. Microsoft sells those tools, so treat the figures as a rough guide, not a lab result.
Count your own interruptions first

Before you change any setting, measure one normal workday. Open a note and add a tally mark each time you leave deep work. Count a Slack ping you act on, a Mac alert you glance at, and a quick Slack check you make on your own. Do not judge yet. The count is your baseline.

Write the time next to every tenth mark. The clusters tell you where to start. A cluster right after a standup needs a different rule than a cluster at 4 pm. Trust your notes over a guess about your own week.
Where each fix lives on your Mac

rows: Silences alerts during a time block you set

Sets when Slack notifies you: every day, weekdays or custom
A schedule you set overrides a default an admin set
Pauses Slack notifications for a set time, such as /dnd for 15 mins
Moves Slack reading to set times
Needs a clear urgent route to work
blocks.caption: Three Slack and Mac controls, plus one habit change.

blocks.text: Set a Focus schedule on your Mac
Apple's Focus feature is already on your Mac. A schedule starts the block without you remembering it. Here is the path in Apple's current guide, which runs System Settings > Focus.

items: Click the Apple menu, then open System Settings.
Click Focus, then select the Focus you want to schedule.
Under Set a Schedule, click Add Schedule.
Choose Time, then enter a start time, an end time and the days.
Click Done. Turn off Schedule at the top to pause it without deleting it.

blocks.text: Focus Filters are a separate section. Apple says they can change how Calendar, Mail, Messages or Safari behave during a Focus. Slack is not on that list. Set Slack on its own, using the steps in the next section.
Set Slack working hours and timed pauses

In Slack, go to Preferences > Working hours. The Allow notifications menu offers Every day, Weekdays or Custom. For Custom, set a start and end time. Slack says a schedule you set overrides any default schedule an admin set for the workspace, so your own hours win.

For a one-off block, type a command in Slack. /dnd for 15 mins pauses alerts for 15 minutes. /dnd until 5pm pauses until 5 pm. /dnd off ends the pause. On desktop you can also click your profile picture, hover over Notifications and pick a timeframe.

blocks.title: A naming check
blocks.text: Slack's help article still says Do Not Disturb, and the /dnd command keeps that name. If a label looks different on your version, search the menu for Notifications or Pause.
Batch your checks without going dark

Batching sounds right, but the evidence is mixed. A Microsoft Research study followed 40 information workers for 12 workdays. It found no evidence that batching email lowered stress. Batching was linked to higher rated productivity when email time was longer.

So batching is a test, not a rule. Pick two or three check times. Put them in your calendar as short blocks. Keep them for one week. Then rate your focus each day and compare it with your Day 1 tally.
Batching fails when nobody knows how to reach you. Keep one urgent route, such as a phone call, so checks can be rare without being risky.
A worked example: one normal Tuesday

Take a typical Tuesday for a product manager. A design review runs in the morning. A sales lead posts a question in a public channel just before lunch. A support rep sends a bug report in a direct message in mid-afternoon. By the end of the day, you have replied to all three, and the spec is still blank.

Now apply the fixes in order. A morning Focus block protects the spec time. Working hours push the sales question to a set check time. A mute on the noisy channel stops the mid-morning pings. The bug report goes to a ticket, not a direct message, and the support rep gets a clear urgent route.
The result is not zero interruptions. The result is fewer, and you choose when they reach you. That is a realistic target for a product manager who works with many stakeholders.
Mistakes that undo the fixes

items: Turning everything off, then missing a real outage or a customer escalation. Keep one route for urgent work.
Setting a Mac Focus but leaving Slack alerts on. Check Slack working hours too.
Setting hours for yourself but not telling the team. Put your check times in your Slack status.
Checking Slack every few minutes to see if you missed something. Set check times, then trust them.
Changing five settings in one day. Change one, run it for a week, then add the next.
Measuring nothing. Without the tally, you cannot tell which fix helped.

blocks.text: When you cannot silence everything

Some weeks need more access. A launch, an incident or a customer escalation may need you live. Plan for those weeks in advance. Agree with your team which messages break through, and how. A phone call or a page works better than a Slack ping during an incident.

blocks.title: Regulated work
blocks.text: If you handle health, legal or financial records, follow your employer rules on client or patient data before you ask any AI tool about it. Keep protected records off the screen while you hold the shortcut.
Where Lazur helps, and where it does not

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. Ask where a control is, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it. Ask how to do something, and Lazur guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click.
Lazur does not change your settings for you. It does not click buttons, mute Slack or turn on Focus. You make each change. Lazur explains the setting, points at it and waits while you click.
Dictation is a useful extra here. Hold fn to dictate a holding reply at the cursor in any app. Dictation is unlimited on both paid plans, and Lazur keeps a memory of what you asked on your Mac.
Next steps for this week

Start with the tally on Day 1. Set the Focus schedule and Slack working hours on the next two days. Run them for a week before you add anything new. For Slack-specific steps, see [Slack for product managers on Mac](/for/product-managers/slack).
You can get Lazur from the [download page](/download). It is a Mac app with a free trial, and no credit card is needed to start. Compare plans on the [pricing page](/pricing) before you decide.

faq.question: Why does Slack keep breaking my focus even after I set a Focus on my Mac?
faq.answer: A Mac Focus controls alerts on your Mac, but Slack keeps its own working hours and notification settings. Check both. Then run a timed block with /dnd and see which pings still get through.

faq.question: How do I pause Slack notifications for 15 minutes?
faq.answer: Type /dnd for 15 mins in Slack. Use /dnd until 5pm to pause until a set time, and /dnd off to end the pause early. On desktop, you can also click your profile picture, hover over Notifications, and pick a timeframe.

faq.question: Does batching Slack checks actually lower stress?
faq.answer: The evidence is weak. A small Microsoft Research study of email found no evidence that batching lowered stress. Treat batching as a test. Track your focus for a week, then keep the schedule only if it helps.

faq.question: What if my manager expects a fast reply?
faq.answer: Tell your manager your check times, and name the messages that need a fast reply. A phone call or a short message in an agreed channel works better than a silent expectation. Agree it once, then write it down.

faq.question: Can Lazur turn off Slack notifications for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons or operate other apps for you. It can explain a setting, point at it, or guide you one click at a time. You make each change yourself.

faq.question: Does Lazur watch my screen all the time?
faq.answer: No. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer them, and Lazur's privacy notes say they are not stored. Follow your employer rules on client or patient data.

faq.question: Are the menu names the same on every Mac?
faq.answer: No. Menu labels can change between macOS versions. Look for the nearest match in System Settings, and check Apple's Set up a Focus page for your version. Slack's help article still uses the older Do Not Disturb name.

faq.question: Does this work on Windows?
faq.answer: The Lazur part does not. Lazur runs on the Mac, on Apple silicon and Intel. Windows is planned, not available. The Slack and Focus steps on this page apply to the Mac.

costs.title: Lost minutes add up fast
costs.text: Microsoft's data says a Microsoft 365 user gets interrupted about every two minutes. A single ping can take seconds to read. The bigger cost is the return, when you rebuild the thread of your thinking. That work does not show up on a calendar.

costs.title: A rough pay figure
costs.text: The BLS lists a May 2025 median of $84.20 per hour for computer and information systems managers. That category is not product managers, so treat it as a proxy. Divide the hourly figure by 60 to price one minute. Use it to justify a schedule, not to measure your worth.

costs.title: Stress and perceived productivity
costs.text: A small Microsoft Research study followed 40 information workers for 12 workdays. Longer daily email time was linked to lower perceived productivity and higher measured stress. The study covered email, not Slack, so read it as a direction, not a verdict.

costs.title: A useful comparison from classrooms
costs.text: A Rutgers study of 118 students in one term found that non-academic device use did not lower in-lecture comprehension. It did lower end-of-term exam scores by at least 5 percent. It is a classroom study, so it does not prove the same effect at work.

causes.title: Slack alerts you the moment a message lands
causes.text: Slack alerts you for direct messages and mentions, and each one arrives with the same sound. A stakeholder question and a bug report sound identical. Nothing in the moment asks which one can wait, so you answer both at once.

causes.title: Chat became the default queue
causes.text: Questions that belong in a ticket or a doc land in direct messages instead. Microsoft's 2025 survey puts the average at 153 Teams messages per weekday. Teams is not Slack, so treat that number as a signal, not a Slack count.

causes.title: Meetings nobody put on a calendar
causes.text: Microsoft's text says 57 percent of meetings are ad hoc calls with no calendar invite. Its methodology gives 60 percent for unscheduled meetings, so the exact share is unclear. Either way, many interruptions have no calendar block to protect you.

causes.title: Nobody can see you are heads down
causes.text: Without a status or a shared Focus, people assume you are free. Apple's Focus guide says you can share that you have silenced notifications, so contacts know you are busy. Without that signal, every ping looks like a fair request.

causes.title: Habit, not messages
causes.text: Some checks have no trigger at all. You open Slack because the quiet feels wrong. Gloria Mark's tracking found people spend an average of 47 seconds on one screen before switching, down from about two and a half minutes in 2004. The urge to switch is fast, and it is easy to act on.

causes.title: No schedule at all
causes.text: If you never set working hours, messages reach you at any hour. Your evening becomes part of the queue, and the next morning starts with a backlog. A schedule does not remove the messages, but it moves them to times you chose.

fixes.title: Use a Focus schedule for deep work
fixes.text: Create a Focus for deep work on your Mac and give it a weekday schedule in System Settings > Focus. The schedule starts on its own, so you do not have to remember it. Pause it with the Schedule switch on the days you need a break.

fixes.title: Set Slack working hours
fixes.text: Open Preferences > Working hours in Slack and choose Every day, Weekdays or Custom. Your own schedule overrides a default an admin set. Tell your team your hours in your status, so they know when to expect a reply.

fixes.title: Use /dnd for one-off blocks
fixes.text: Type /dnd for 15 mins before a design review, or /dnd until 5pm for the rest of an afternoon. Type /dnd off to end the pause early. This covers the moments a schedule misses, like an unplanned deep-work afternoon.

fixes.title: Mute the noisiest channels
fixes.text: List the three channels that send the most pings. Mute them, then check them at set times. Keep direct messages from your manager and your engineering lead on, since those usually need a quick reply.

fixes.title: Write a status that names the route
fixes.text: A status such as heads down until 3 pm, urgent issues go to my phone tells people what to do. It does more than say you are busy. Update it when your block ends, so the status does not go stale.

fixes.title: Move repeat questions to one place
fixes.text: Answer the same question once in a doc, a Linear issue or a Slack channel, then link to it. For a dedicated space, see [how to create a channel in Slack](/how-to/create-a-channel-in-slack). Repeat questions cost the most, because each one restarts a thread.

fixes.title: Batch checks at set times
fixes.text: Check Slack at a few set times, such as after standup, after lunch and before you log off. Batching has mixed evidence, so test it for a week and compare your own focus ratings with the week before.

fixes.title: Tally your interruptions every week
fixes.text: Keep the same simple tally for one week, then for the next. If the count did not drop, change one setting and test again. Small changes are easier to judge than a full overhaul.

fixes.title: Agree an urgent route with your team
fixes.text: Name the messages that can break through, such as a live outage or a customer escalation. Pick one route, such as a phone call. Write it down, so no one has to guess during an incident.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Count your interruptions
plan.text: Keep a tally in a note for one normal workday. Add a mark each time you leave deep work for Slack, a Mac alert or a quick check. Change nothing yet, so the baseline stays clean.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Set a Focus schedule
plan.text: Open System Settings > Focus. Create a Focus for deep work, add a schedule for one morning block, then confirm it turns on at the set time.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Set Slack working hours
plan.text: Open Preferences > Working hours in Slack. Choose Weekdays or Custom. Mute the noisiest channels, and keep direct messages from your manager turned on.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Write your status and urgent route
plan.text: Set a Slack status that names your next check time and the urgent route. Agree the route with your team, so no one guesses during an incident.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Move repeat questions
plan.text: Answer the most common question once in a doc, a Linear issue or a channel, then link to it. Stop answering it again in direct messages.

plan.label: Day 6
plan.title: Batch your checks
plan.text: Pick two or three check times and keep them. Let the Focus schedule run. Skip checks outside those times unless the urgent route fires.

plan.label: Day 7
plan.title: Compare and keep what works
plan.text: Count interruptions again and compare the total with Day 1. Keep the settings that cut the count, and drop any that delay a reply that matters.
